paras: The attempted lynching of the Lebanon Cemetery body snatchers took place in Philadelphia on December 5, 1882, when a crowd of Black residents outside a magistrate's office threatened to lynch four men charged with stealing bodies from a Black burial ground. Police held off two rushes and took the prisoners to the Central station, and the wire carried the story under headlines such as "The Ghouls Nearly Lynched."

On the night of December 4, reporters of the Philadelphia Press and a Pinkerton operative stopped an express wagon carrying corpses and arrested Frank McNamee, Henry "Dutch" Pillet and Levi Chew, who was described as colored. The bodies had been taken from Lebanon Cemetery, "a burying ground for colored persons," and were bound for dissection at Jefferson College. The next morning detectives arrested Levi's brother Robert Chew, the cemetery's superintendent, and Andrew Mullen.

Long before the 4 p.m. hearing before Magistrate Lennon, "crowds of colored people" blockaded Seventh street, and plots to lynch the prisoners on their arrival were discussed. Constable Myers and Pinkerton detective Henderson rushed the men through a back door, and the crowd answered with jeers and yells. Inside, Robert Chew's statement that he had been paid three dollars a body, and burial records showing some fifty-five bodies in one grave, caused a sensation.

When the prisoners were held for a further hearing, the crowd made "an overwhelming rush" for the entry and gateway "with threats to lynch the prisoners," and Sergeant Brode and ten reserves were sent for. On a second rush, men and women struck at the captives, and the police drew their clubs and went almost at a trot down Chestnut street to the Central station, where the men were locked up for the night. No injuries were reported, and no one in the crowd is reported arrested.

In the following days crowds dug up graves at Lebanon Cemetery in search of their dead, and a call went out for an indignation meeting at Liberty Hall, where "trouble is feared." At the meeting on December 7, Black speakers thanked the Press for the arrests, and razors and revolvers were drawn when cemetery trustee Burton appeared before clergymen restored order.

McNamee confessed and named Dr. William S. Forbes of Jefferson Medical College as the instigator. On December 15 McNamee and Pillet pleaded guilty, the two Chews were tried and found guilty, and Forbes and an assistant were held in $6,000 each.

The episode reached readers mainly through a single wire dispatch dated December 5, printed the next day in papers from Savannah to St. Paul and Washington. Editors put the lynching threat into the display lines: the Savannah Morning News ran "The Ghouls Nearly Lynched," the St. Paul Globe "Attempts to Lynch," and the National Republican "Threats of Lynching." The Wilmington Daily Gazette carried the fullest version, in which the prisoners "shrank and cowered like hunted rats."

Later accounts drew more attention to race: the Wheeling Register headed its story "Razors and Pistols" and described Levi Chew as a "coal-black darkey" called "Charcoal." A brief in the Huntsville Gazette on December 16 said four "colored resurrectionists" had needed twenty-five policemen to protect them "from a mob of their own race."

Accounts differ on details: the St. Paul Globe gave bail as $1,000 against $5,000 elsewhere, and the Huntsville Gazette's twenty-five policemen and four colored prisoners differ from the Philadelphia accounts of ten reserves and two white defendants. The Wheeling Register placed razors and revolvers outside the magistrate's office, while the National Republican reported them drawn at the Liberty Hall meeting two days later.

bases: A crowd outside the magistrate's office rushed the entry with threats to lynch four men held on body-snatching charges and struck at them until police clubbed a way to the station (A1, A2, A4).

No one was killed: a crowd threatened to lynch and struck at the prisoners over the robbing of a colored cemetery, but police got them to the Central station (A1, A2, A10); it was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
The wire report (A2, A3, A4), the Wilmington Gazette's fuller version (A1) and a separate Dec. 7 dispatch (A8) agree on the crowd, the threats to lynch and the police escort.
